clue.text: Comedians in show to enter in disguise

indicators.note: something in disguise is made to look different, so these letters appear in a changed order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Performers in a show sneak onto the stage wearing costumes.
explanation.walkthrough: THE TWO RONNIES were the British TV comedy double act of Ronnie Barker and Ronnie Corbett. 'Comedians in show' looks like one phrase, but 'in' belongs to the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The title names a famous pair of British television comics, so they are literally comedians.

clue.text: Issue raised over this writer's plaque ages ago

definitions.note: the answer is a noun phrase usually meaning 'a very long time ago', as in 'from time immemorial'

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising a word means reading it from the bottom upwards, so it is turned around

parts.note: to emit is to issue or send out
the setter refers to themselves: this writer is = I'M
a memorial plaque commemorates someone

explanation.surface: A writer commemorated by a plaque that went up long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over' simply places the reversed word on top of the rest in this down clue. 'This writer's' is read as 'this writer is', the setter's I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Time immemorial is a period so remote that nobody can remember it, i.e. ages ago.

clue.text: Old comic that's below par

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a British boys' comic paper of the 1950s and 60s featuring Dan Dare
second meaning: in golf, a hole completed in two strokes under par

explanation.surface: An elderly comedian whose act is now substandard.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Comic' suggests a comedian and 'below par' suggests poor form; in fact one is a magazine and the other a golf score.
explanation.definitionFit: The Eagle was a famous British children's comic paper, and an eagle in golf is a score of two strokes under par.

clue.text: Places you'll find spare tyres, reportedly rubbish brands

indicators.note: reportedly means as it is said or heard, so we want a word that sounds like the next phrase

parts.note: waste is rubbish, and lines are product ranges or brands

explanation.surface: Discarded car tyres pile up where poor-quality brands are dumped.
explanation.walkthrough: A spare tyre is jocular slang for a roll of fat around the middle, which is where it sits on the body.
explanation.definitionFit: A spare tyre of belly fat is carried around the waist, so waistlines are where you find it.

clue.text: Object wearing torn old clothing

indicators.note: someone wearing something has it around them, so one word is placed inside the other

parts.note: rent is the past tense of rend, to tear
an aim is an object or goal

explanation.surface: Some item dressed in ragged, aged garments.
explanation.walkthrough: Here the word for torn wears the object: it goes around it.
explanation.definitionFit: Raiment is an archaic, literary word for garments, hence 'old' clothing.

clue.text: Money saved from temping gets entirely used up

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the letters are read from the bottom upwards, so they run backwards
from says the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows, not built up

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the end of the first word, all of the second and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A temp worker's savings all get spent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Entirely' looks like it qualifies 'used up', but its first letters are part of the hidden run, which then reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A nest egg is a sum of money put aside for the future, such as retirement savings.

clue.text: Desire entrancing female? Get rid of wife!

indicators.note: getting rid of something removes it, so a letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: a witch casts spells, so she is an entrancing (bewitching) woman
W is the standard abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: A man tempted by a captivating woman decides to ditch his spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: Entrancing is read literally: casting a spell, as a witch does. Removing W leaves the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An itch is a restless craving or desire, as in an itch to travel.

clue.text: Character has doubts occasionally with unknown tax

parts.note: stamp means nature or character, as in 'a man of his stamp'

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so only every other letter of the word is kept

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters
in algebra x, y and z stand for unknowns

explanation.surface: Someone is uncertain now and then about an unexplained levy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Has' and 'with' just glue the pieces together. STAMP DUTY is a British tax, notably paid on buying property.
explanation.definitionFit: Stamp duty is a government levy charged on certain documents and transactions, so it is a tax.

clue.text: Author Chris slackened working

indicators.note: working suggests being put into action and reshaped, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A writer called Chris eased off on the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Author Chris' reads as a named writer, but Chris is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Charles Dickens was the Victorian novelist who wrote Oliver Twist and Great Expectations, so a famous author.

clue.text: Makes great flipping scene outwardly whenever in school

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the whole string built here is read backwards
outwardly points to the outside of the word, so only its first and last letters are kept

parts.note: the outside letters
if can mean whenever, as in 'if it rains, we stay in'
taken as written
a gam is a school of whales

explanation.surface: Someone exaggerates by making a dramatic scene whenever they are at school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British expletive, but it reverses everything after it. GAM is a whaling word for a school of whales.
explanation.definitionFit: To magnify is to make something larger, so it makes things great in size.

clue.text: Jar with money left inside

indicators.note: inside says one piece sits within another, so the single letter goes into the word

parts.note: cash is money
L is the abbreviation for left

explanation.surface: A savings jar with some coins left in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jar' looks like a container noun, but it is a verb: to grate or conflict.
explanation.definitionFit: Colours or opinions that jar are incompatible and conflict, which is what clash means as a verb.

clue.text: Bungling current record attempt ultimately

parts.note: in means fashionable or current
an EP is an extended-play record

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is used

parts.note: the last letter

explanation.surface: A clumsy, failed attempt at a recent record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' tempts I, the physics symbol for current, but here it means fashionable.
explanation.definitionFit: Inept means lacking skill, so a bungling effort is an inept one.

clue.text: Fair number heading off

indicators.note: with its heading off, the word loses its first letter

parts.note: seven is a number

explanation.surface: A reasonable sum, leaving out the headline figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' is the vaguest of hints; the deletion narrows it to a number beginning with a spare letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Even can mean fair or balanced, as in an even contest or an even chance.

clue.text: Knocks over box

indicators.note: turned over means turned back to front, so the word is read in reverse

parts.note: raps are sharp knocks

explanation.surface: A boxer knocks an opponent down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocks over' reads as one phrasal verb, but 'over' is the reversal signal and 'box' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To spar is to box in practice, trading punches without full force.

clue.text: Staggering effort penning article on that woman's ancestor

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, as in a pen, so one piece is written inside another
staggering means lurching unsteadily, so the letters reel into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
a is the indefinite article
her is the possessive for a woman

explanation.surface: An amazing effort to write a piece about her family tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Staggering' looks like praise for the effort, but it shuffles it. 'On' places the last piece after the rest in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A forefather is a forebear, someone from whom a person is descended, i.e. an ancestor.

clue.text: Left-winger in team vacated spot month before

parts.note: Mar is the short form of March
a cricket or football team has eleven players, written XI

indicators.note: a vacated place has been emptied, so the middle of the word goes and only its outside letters remain

parts.note: the outside letters

explanation.surface: A left-winger in a sports team has left a position free.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Month before' places the month ahead of the other pieces; 'in' is just a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Marxist follows Karl Marx's communist ideas, so sits on the political left.

clue.text: Out of practice state distrust in essential nurses

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold closely, so the phrase before it carries the answer within it

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the three words

explanation.surface: Mistrust is a basic problem that nursing staff face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nurses' reads as a noun, but it is a verb meaning holds.
explanation.definitionFit: Rustiness is the condition of skills that have slipped from lack of use, a state of being out of practice.

clue.text: Ball from good lofted shot ruled out of bounds

parts.note: G is the abbreviation for good
a lob is a shot hit high into the air

indicators.note: without its bounds the word loses its edges, so only its middle letters are kept

parts.note: the inner letters

explanation.surface: A tennis umpire rules that a high shot landed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Out of bounds' sounds like an umpire's call, but it trims the word before it.
explanation.definitionFit: A globule is a small round drop, a tiny ball of liquid.

clue.text: Gains control over golf tournament

definitions.meaning: first meaning: becomes the master of, as of a skill or a situation
second meaning: the annual major championship held at Augusta, Georgia

explanation.surface: A golfer takes command of a big championship.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means subdues or learns thoroughly, and the Augusta major is officially named after this word.

clue.text: Rearrange dance

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to mix up the order, as with a pack of cards
second meaning: a dance of sliding, dragging steps

explanation.definitionFit: A pack is mixed up by this action, and a dance with dragging feet across the floor bears the same name.

clue.text: Oddly, Phil every new day would get drunk

indicators.note: oddly points to the odd-numbered positions, so the first, third, fifth letters and so on are kept

parts.note: the odd-placed letters of the three words run together
D is the abbreviation for day

explanation.surface: A man named Phil goes out drinking every single day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Oddly' sounds like a comment on Phil's behaviour. PIE-EYED is informal for very drunk.
explanation.definitionFit: Pie-eyed is a slang word for intoxicated, describing someone with glazed eyes from drink.

clue.text: Saw bishop parking car previously

parts.note: P is the road-sign abbreviation for parking
Rover was a British car make
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: A bishop had parked his car earlier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Previously' puts the parking and car pieces ahead of the bishop. 'Saw' looks like the past tense of see, but it is a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old saying, a maxim, which is exactly what a proverb is.

clue.text: Attack American papers pursuing Republican

parts.note: R is the abbreviation for Republican
A is the abbreviation for American
ID papers are identity documents

explanation.surface: Someone attacks US newspapers that are chasing a Republican politician.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pursuing' means coming after, so the American papers follow the Republican.
explanation.definitionFit: A raid is a sudden assault on a place, so it is an attack.

clue.text: Brief role pressing case for underrated sport

indicators.note: pressing means squeezing tightly around, so one piece is held within the other
something brief is cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: a job is a role

indicators.note: a case is the outside covering of something, so only the outer letters of the next word are used

parts.note: the outer letters

explanation.surface: A minor part in a film argues the case for an overlooked sport.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brief role' reads as a cameo, but 'brief' trims the word for role.
explanation.definitionFit: Judo is a Japanese martial art practised competitively as an Olympic sport.

clue.text: Miscreant I conclude is inspiring caper

indicators.note: inspiring here means breathing in, so the preceding words take the answer inside them

parts.note: a run of letters spanning the first three words

explanation.surface: A villain decides a crime was his inspiration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inspiring' is read literally as drawing in, holding the letters within.
explanation.definitionFit: An antic is a playful or absurd act, a prank or caper.

clue.text: Feeling irritated, at heart that hurt

indicators.note: the heart of a word is its centre, so only its middle letter is kept

parts.note: the middle letter of nine
the cry someone gives when something hurts

explanation.surface: A person feels annoyed, deep down, that something was painful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That hurt' is read as the exclamation a person makes when hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Touch is the sense of feeling things through the skin, so the noun feeling fits.

clue.text: Defensive line formed by half-cut London footballers

indicators.note: half-cut means half removed, so one half of the name is dropped

parts.note: Millwall is a football club in south-east London

explanation.surface: Drunk London football fans form a defensive line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-cut' is British slang for drunk, which the surface uses; the clue takes it literally.
explanation.definitionFit: In football, a wall is the row of defenders lining up to block a free kick, so a defensive line.

clue.text: Ground nuts near starter of anchovies

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, so the letters go wild and are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a starter comes first, so only the opening letter of the next word is used

parts.note: the first letter

explanation.surface: A recipe: ground nuts placed beside an anchovy appetiser.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ground nuts' reads as a cooking ingredient, but 'Ground' is the definition and 'nuts' the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An arena is a sports ground or stadium where events are held.

clue.text: Pub and empty hotel next to river

parts.note: free means unoccupied, as in a free seat
H is hotel in the NATO phonetic alphabet
the Ouse is an English river

explanation.surface: A pub and a deserted hotel stand by the riverside.
explanation.walkthrough: A free house is a British pub not tied to one brewery, so it can sell any beer.
explanation.definitionFit: A free house is a type of pub that is independent of brewery ownership.

clue.text: Rogue lives close to sister and flogs trees

indicators.note: rogue means behaving wildly out of line, so the letters go astray into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the close of a word is its end, so only its last letter is kept

parts.note: the last letter
to birch is to flog with a bundle of twigs

explanation.surface: A villain lives near his sister and whips people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rogue' reads as a noun for the villain, but it is the anagram signal; 'close to sister' joins the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Silver birches are white-barked trees common across northern Europe.
